porbos.title: Those Whose Hands Were Tied • The Qur’an Speaks of Those Days • The Same Note in Makkan Verses • Permission Came • Courtesy Even in War

blocks.1: One day in Makkah some Companions came to the Prophet {{1}}. One of them was ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf (RA). They had one thing to say.
blocks.3: O Messenger of Allah, when we were polytheists, we were in honour. And when we believed, we became humiliated. The Messenger of Allah {{1}} said, I have been commanded to forgive; so do not fight.{{2}}
blocks.4: A Muslim is being beaten, his house is being broken, he is being boycotted; and he is being told, do not raise a hand. Those who had been in honour while polytheists, after faith were not permitted even to raise a hand when they were beaten.
blocks.5: This was said not once. For thirteen years they had to hear this very thing. Thirteen years, every day of which began with the same question, will the limit break today? The Prophet {{1}} had only one answer. Patience. One form of courage we all know; the one who leaps in. Another form is hard to recognise; the one who waits, though knowing that strength is in their hands. These thirteen years of Makkah were training in the second kind of courage.
blocks.6: The Qur’an Speaks of Those Days
blocks.7: When the command of war came after coming to Madinah, the Qur’an brought up those days of the past again.
blocks.9: Have you not seen those who (in Makkan life) were told, restrain your hands, establish prayer and give zakat? Then when fighting was prescribed for them, a group of them began to fear people (the enemies) as one fears Allah, or even more. They began to say, our Lord! Why did You prescribe fighting for us? Why did You not give us respite for a short while? Say, the enjoyment of this world is little. For the one who adopts taqwa, the Hereafter is better. You will not be wronged even by a thread.{{1}}
blocks.10: The occasion of revelation of this verse is also that very same incident.
blocks.12: Then when Allah moved us to Madinah, He commanded fighting; but they drew back their hands. Then Allah revealed, ‘Have you not seen those who were told, restrain your hands and establish prayer’.{{1}}
blocks.13: What happened in their hearts? Were the Companions afraid? After bearing thirteen years of oppression and coming to Madinah, they had got a breath of some peace. Then it occurred to some that it would have been good if the command of war had come some time later. This was not an objection to Allah’s command. This was entirely a human desire. And the standing of the Companions of the Prophet {{1}} is far above all this.{{2}}
blocks.14: What was the meaning of that thirteen years of patience? In Makkah the Muslims were bearing harsh oppression. In many minds a desire for revenge would arise. But the command of jihad had not yet come. Good was placed in patience and self-restraint, so that they might acquire the qualities of noble character. Because the fighting afterwards would then not be personal revenge; it would be for the pleasure of Allah.{{1}}
blocks.15: This is the account of thirteen years. Had the sword come first, it would have been revenge. Coming after patience, it became justice.
blocks.16: The Same Note in Makkan Verses
blocks.17: The patience of these thirteen years did not rest only on the Prophet’s {{1}} spoken word. Surah ash-Shura, revealed in Makkah, has drawn its picture too; while counting the qualities of the believers, it said,
blocks.19: And those who avoid major sins and shameful deeds, and when their anger arises, forgive.{{1}}
blocks.20: Anger arises; the Qur’an did not deny this. The only question is, after it arises, what does the person do.{{1}}
blocks.21: Anger makes a person blind and deaf. They forget the difference between right and wrong. The quality of the believer is that even in anger they keep the limit; and they give up even their own rightful claim.{{1}}
blocks.22: And another verse of this very surah states a rule that applies everywhere, from the battlefield to a quarrel at home.
blocks.24: The recompense of an evil is an evil like it. But whoever forgives and makes amends, their reward rests with Allah. Surely He does not love the wrongdoers.{{1}}
blocks.25: The recompense is like for like; not more than that. As much hurt as the oppressor has caused, the oppressed too may cause that much; in no way more than this. And this recompense is only a right. In the very next sentence it says, if one is patient and forgives the oppressor, that is an even more virtuous deed.{{1}}
blocks.26: But there is also a balance. For an oppressor who is remorseful, forgiving is better. And for one who persists and continues the oppression, taking recompense may be better. But recompense is only in something that is not itself a sin. If someone is forced to drink wine, they too cannot make another drink wine.{{1}}
blocks.27: And the last verse of this part is short, but weighty.
blocks.29: In truth, whoever is patient and forgives, this is an act of great resolve.{{1}}
blocks.30: An act of great resolve. Forgiveness is not the work of the weak; in the Qur’an’s reckoning it is an act of resolve. Those thirteen years of Makkah were therefore not years of weakness. Those who had been in honour while polytheists were the ones holding back their hands there. This is the difference between response and revenge. The response that observes measure is justice. The response that exceeds measure is revenge. Taking recompense is a right, forgiving is a virtue. There is a just response. There is saying the just word with patience at the right time. And there is giving back in a fit of anger merely for the sake of giving back; whose aim is to harm the person, not to correct the wrong. The urge for revenge and the pleasure of Allah are not the same thing.
blocks.32: Behind the first verse in which permission for war came after coming to Madinah lies a broken heart. The time of leaving Makkah. Out of home, out of city; and the offence only one, they had said, our Lord is Allah.
blocks.34: When the Prophet {{1}} was driven out of Makkah, Abu Bakr (RA) said, they have driven out their Prophet; inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji‘un, they will surely be destroyed. Then it was revealed, ‘Permission is given to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged; Allah is fully able to help them.’ Abu Bakr (RA) said, I understood, there will be fighting. Ibn ‘Abbas said, this is the first verse revealed about fighting.{{2}}
blocks.35: A sentence coming out of the chest. They will be destroyed. And in reply, from Allah’s side, the verse that came, its very words can be seen.
blocks.37: Permission is given to those who are being fought (they may fight in their own defence). Because they have been wronged. Know for certain that Allah is fully able to give them victory. Those who have been driven out of their homes unjustly, only because they said, our Lord is Allah. Had Allah not repelled one group of mankind (their harm) by means of another, the monasteries, churches, houses of worship and mosques, in which Allah’s name is remembered abundantly, would have been demolished. Allah will surely help those who help Him (His din). Surely Allah is All-Strong, Mighty.{{1}}
blocks.38: ‘In defence’; ‘wronged’; ‘driven out unjustly’. A reason is placed in every word of the permission. In these two verses two things. The first. In Makkah for a full thirteen years the believers had the command of patience and restraint, and they obeyed it with the highest sacrifice. However harsh the persecution, there was no permission to confront it with weapons. It was in this very verse for the first time that permission to raise the sword came. Before this, in many verses fighting was prohibited.{{1}}
blocks.39: The second. In this verse the significance of jihad is stated. All the prophets and messengers who came in the world built places of worship. Without permission for jihad, the opponents of places of worship would have wiped out all the places of worship.{{1}}
blocks.40: In the very next verse the purpose of the sword has become even clearer.
blocks.42: They are those who, if I give them power in the land, will establish prayer, pay zakat, enjoin good and forbid wrong. And the outcome of all matters is in Allah’s hands.{{1}}
blocks.43: What will they do if given power; prayer, zakat, enjoining good, forbidding wrong. In this there is no mention of wealth or land or revenge. This is the reason for the assurance of help in building an Islamic state in Madinah and in jihad against the disbelievers. If these people get power, they will spend life and wealth to build an environment of worship. In this way, in this very verse the fundamental aim of the Islamic state has been stated.{{1}}
blocks.44: This verse was revealed right after the Hijrah, when Muslims had power nowhere on earth. ‘Uthman (RA) said, the verse praised them before the deed. Later the caliphs from among the Muhajirun came to power and did exactly that.{{1}}
blocks.45: The question of what we would do if given power is in our homes too. Our powers are small. One is a father, one a headmaster, one a boss at the office, one a shop owner. When that small power comes into our hands, what do we do? Do we give our subordinates time for prayer, or not? Do we obstruct good, or help?
blocks.47: Along with permission, the Qur’an also stated the limit.
blocks.49: Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Know for certain that Allah does not love transgressors.{{1}}
blocks.50: It has been decided in this very verse; fighting is to be only with those who are fighting. And if the limit is broken, Allah will not love. The Prophet {{1}} himself taught the explanation of that limit. When sending off a commander, the words he would say to them, calling them aside separately, Buraydah (RA) has remembered.
blocks.52: When the Messenger of Allah {{1}} appointed anyone commander of an army or expedition, he would particularly advise them to fear Allah and to treat the Muslims with them well. Then he would say, fight in the name of Allah, in the way of Allah. Fight whoever has rejected Allah. Fight, but do not misappropriate the spoils, do not break treaties, do not mutilate the dead, and do not kill any child.{{2}}
blocks.53: Four prohibitions. No misappropriation, no treachery, no desecration of the dead, no taking a child’s life. Near the end of the same hadith there is another instruction about promises. During the siege of a fortress, if the enemy asks for protection in the name of Allah and His Prophet, what will be the commander’s answer?
blocks.55: When you besiege the people of a fortress and they want you to give them the protection of Allah and His Prophet, do not give them the protection of Allah and His Prophet; rather give them your own protection and the protection of your companions. Because breaking your own protection is lighter than breaking the protection of Allah and His Messenger.{{1}}
blocks.56: He regarded the burden of giving a word so heavily that he did not want to place even the slightest risk of breaking it upon the name of Allah and the Messenger. And the last sentence of the same hadith is even deeper.
blocks.58: And when you besiege the people of a fortress, and they want you to bring them down on the judgement of Allah, do not bring them down on the judgement of Allah; rather bring them down on your own judgement. Because you do not know whether you will get Allah’s judgement about them right.{{1}}
blocks.59: The commander will take his decision in his own name. Before putting it through by saying ‘this is Allah’s judgement’, he has to respect his own limits. Two groups quarrel over a ruling. One says, what I have understood is Allah’s judgement. The other says, you have understood wrongly. Within a few days the quarrel slides into abuse, the abuse into factions. Even the commander who really had weapons in hand was taught, do not put through your own decision as Allah’s judgement. How much of this humility do we keep in places of disagreement? In one expedition the body of a woman was found. The incident has been told by Ibn ‘Umar (RA).
blocks.61: In one of the battles of the Messenger of Allah {{1}} a woman was found killed. Then the Messenger of Allah {{2}} forbade the killing of women and children.{{3}}
blocks.62: The death of a woman on the battlefield. After that death, a prohibition. Even on the battlefield the lives of women and children were forbidden; and misappropriation, treachery, desecration of the dead too. When we enter a quarrel, do we observe that limit? Whom I am angry with, their parents, their family, their past; do I have permission to drag these in?
blocks.63: Another thing has been said, which we often avoid.
blocks.65: Fighting (with the enemy) has been prescribed for you, though it is disliked by you. It is quite possible that you dislike a thing, though it is good for you. And it is also possible that you like a thing, though it is bad for you. And (the real matter) Allah knows, and you do not know.{{1}}
blocks.66: ‘Disliked by you.’ In the very verse of prescribing war it is admitted, this is not anyone’s favourite thing. ‘Disliked’ means feeling difficult and heavy to the self. It does not mean that the command seems irrational. So there is no fault in this much. What is dearer to a person than life? Then what task could be harder than war! The steps are also clear. In Makkah there was no permission for war. After the Hijrah permission came, but only against those who are fighting the Muslims.{{1}}
blocks.67: In the very religion that has the command of war, war is called ‘not liked’. The believer’s position is between these two. The Prophet {{1}} stated this dislikedness of war in a speech as well.
blocks.69: On a day of facing the enemy, the Messenger of Allah {{1}} waited until the sun declined, then stood among the people and said, O people! Do not wish to meet the enemy, ask Allah for safety. And when you meet them, be patient, and know that Paradise is under the shade of swords.{{2}}
blocks.70: First not wishing, first asking for safety. And when it comes upon them, patience. A religion that gives permission for war and says in the same breath, ‘do not wish for war’, its sword is never an instrument of revenge.

Forgiveness is only for the weak, the strong will take recompense

The trade route of Quraysh needs to be seized, so permission

They will go back to Makkah again

quiz.q: You are an office boss; according to Surah al-Hajj 22:41, what is the right use of power?

Being patient on facing the enemy
Warning the enemy before the war

quiz.q: During a siege of a fortress, which protection is the commander told to give?

Their own and their companions’ protection; not the protection of Allah and the Messenger
No protection at all; because protection does not work during war

quiz.q: What is the reason for the prohibition of bringing down the enemy ‘on the judgement of Allah’?

quiz.q: What does the dars say about dragging the opponent’s family and past into a quarrel?

quiz.q: When there is disagreement in a ruling, what is the dars’s lesson about saying ‘my understanding is Allah’s judgement’?
o: Abusing the opponent is permissible whenever there is disagreement

Treating one’s own understanding as decisive and forcing everyone to follow it
Leaving everyone and becoming alone when there is disagreement

porbos.title: A Year With No Expedition • The Sword Outside, the Hand Inside • Three Small Groups • Raid on Madinah’s Pastures • The Secret Letter

blocks.1: Now the story of the expeditions. But at the start a fact that overturns many people’s idea. After coming to Madinah the Prophet {{1}} did not go out on any expedition for a full year. He first went out in the month of Safar, twelve months after coming to Madinah.
blocks.3: After coming to Madinah the Messenger of Allah {{1}} stayed in Madinah for the rest of the month of Rabi‘ al-Awwal, Rabi‘ al-Thani, the two Jumadas, Rajab, Sha‘ban, Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa‘dah and Dhu al-Hijjah; that Hajj was led by the polytheists; and Muharram. Then in the month of Safar, at the head of twelve months from coming to Madinah, he went out on an expedition. He went as far as Waddan; this is the Battle of al-Abwa’. He had Quraysh and Banu Damrah in view. Banu Damrah made a pact with him, and the pact was made by their chief Makhshi ibn ‘Amr al-Damri. He returned to Madinah, having met no harm.{{2}}
blocks.4: The result of the whole journey was a pact. In this one year in Madinah the mosque was built, brotherhood was made, the charter was made. The expedition came after that. Sa‘d ibn ‘Ubadah (RA) stayed in Madinah; the white banner was in the hand of uncle Hamzah (RA).{{1}}
blocks.5: This was the wording of the pact with Banu Damrah. Their lives and property would be safe. If anyone attacked them the Muslims would help; but not if they rebelled against Allah’s din. If the Prophet {{1}} called them for help, they too had to respond.{{2}}
blocks.6: These expeditions were like this from the start. There is going out, there is returning, but no blood.
blocks.7: The Sword Outside, the Hand Inside
blocks.8: After this, several more expeditions one after another. The picture of all of them is almost the same. What was the purpose of these expeditions? To learn the condition of the surroundings of Madinah and the road to Makkah. To make pacts with the tribes on the way. And to let Quraysh, the polytheists of Yathrib and the Jews know that the Muslims were not weak now. The aim was that Quraysh might incline toward peace.{{1}}
blocks.9: In Rabi‘ al-Awwal, Buwat. He went out with two hundred riders, the target was a trade caravan of Quraysh, which had Umayyah ibn Khalaf and a hundred men and two and a half thousand camels. He went as far as Buwat and returned, having met no harm.{{1}}
blocks.10: Then in Jumada al-Ula, ‘Ushayrah. This time he stayed away more than a month; at a place named ‘Ushayrah in Yanbu‘. In this expedition there were only thirty camels as mounts, the Companions would ride in turns.{{1}}
blocks.12: Then he halted at ‘Ushayrah in the lowland of Yanbu‘; there he stayed the month of Jumada al-Ula and some nights of Jumada al-Ukhra. There he made a pact with Banu Mudlij and their allies Banu Damrah. Then he returned to Madinah, having met no harm.{{1}}
blocks.13: Another pact. Another return. This ‘Ushayrah is mentioned in a sound hadith too. Zayd ibn Arqam (RA) was asked, how many ghazwahs did the Prophet {{1}} go on?
blocks.15: He said, nineteen. It was asked, in how many were you with him? He said, seventeen. I asked, which of them was the first? He said, al-‘Usayrah, or al-‘Ushayr.{{1}}
blocks.16: Zayd (RA) is saying that the first expedition he himself went on was ‘Ushayrah.{{1}}
blocks.17: In this same ‘Ushayrah another incident happens. The name ‘Abu Turab’. ‘Ali and ‘Ammar (RA) had fallen asleep on the ground. The Prophet {{1}} woke them by nudging with his foot. Seeing dust on ‘Ali’s body he said, ‘Abu Turab’.{{2}}
blocks.18: Behind the name, that sleeping ground.
blocks.20: Meanwhile separately some small groups had also gone out. These are called sariyyah. The commander of one group was Hamzah (RA). With him thirty Muhajirun, a white banner, the target a caravan of Quraysh.
blocks.22: The Messenger of Allah {{1}} tied a white banner for Hamzah ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib (RA); with thirty Muhajirun, to block the path of Quraysh’s caravan. Hamzah (RA) met Abu Jahl; Abu Jahl had three hundred men of Quraysh. Majdi ibn ‘Amr stepped in between the two sides, so no fighting took place between them.{{2}}
blocks.23: Thirty against three hundred. In between, a peacemaker stepped in. Everyone returned. The banner of this group was white.{{1}}
blocks.24: The commander of another group was ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Harith (RA); sixty Muhajirun, not one of them an Ansari.
blocks.26: The Messenger of Allah {{1}} tied a white banner for ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Harith (RA) and told him to go toward Batn Rabigh. With sixty Muhajirun he reached Thaniyyat al-Murrah near al-Juhfah; none of them was an Ansari. There, at a spring named Ahya’, he faced a group of Quraysh. Between them there was only an exchange of arrows; there was no leaping on each other with swords.{{2}}
blocks.27: An exchange of arrows; nothing more. That day in the group of Quraysh itself there were two Muslims, al-Miqdad ibn ‘Amr and ‘Utbah ibn Ghazwan (RA). They had not been able to migrate, being under the disbelievers’ control. Getting the chance, they left the group of Quraysh and joined the Muslims.{{1}}
blocks.28: And within this exchange, one arrow has taken a place in Arab history.
blocks.30: I am the first of the Arabs to shoot an arrow in the way of Allah. And when we went to battle with the Prophet {{1}}, we had nothing to eat except the leaves of trees.{{2}}
blocks.31: In which expedition Sa‘d (RA) said this is known from the incident of ‘Ubaydah’s sariyyah. There he shot an arrow, the first on the side of the Islamic force. And how much hardship even the first arrow of the Arabs was shot through is captured in the very words of that hadith.{{1}}
blocks.32: The leader of another group was Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas (RA) himself.
blocks.34: (Sa‘d (RA) says) I went out on foot with some men. We would hide by day and travel by night, and finally on the morning of the fifth day we reached al-Kharrar. The Messenger of Allah {{1}} had taken a promise from me, not to go beyond al-Kharrar. But the caravan had passed before me, a day earlier.{{2}}
blocks.35: A five-day journey. Walking at night, hiding by day. And when they arrived, the caravan had gone a day earlier. Still he did not cross the limit of al-Kharrar. He said, I have received the command; up to al-Kharrar. One picture of observing the limit of a command. Even the temptation of being able to catch the caravan did not pull him beyond that limit.{{1}}
blocks.36: For us too there is a limit of command; in work, in the household, in din. The gain from crossing the limit is actually a loss.
blocks.38: One day the enemy itself came to the door of Madinah.
blocks.40: After returning from ‘Ushayrah the Messenger of Allah {{1}} stayed in Madinah a few nights, fewer than ten. Then Kurz ibn Jabir al-Fihri raided the pasture of Madinah. The Messenger of Allah {{2}} went out in pursuit of him and reached a valley named Safwan on the side of Badr; this is called Badr al-Ula. Kurz slipped from his hand.{{3}}
blocks.41: The herd of animals on Madinah’s pasture was looted. The Prophet {{1}} gave chase, but the man fled. This time the enemy itself had come looking. Four expeditions had now taken place. al-Abwa’, Buwat, ‘Ushayrah and this Badr al-Ula. The Prophet {{2}} himself went on all of them. At the end of the first three the same sentence: returned, having met no harm. In two of them the result was one pact each.{{3}}
blocks.42: Zayd ibn Harithah (RA) had been left as deputy in Madinah.{{1}}
blocks.44: After all these small expeditions came that sariyyah, whose incident put the Muslims into a painful test. The month of Rajab. After returning to Madinah. The Prophet {{1}} sent ‘Abdullah ibn Jahsh (RA) with eight Muhajirun companions. There was no Ansari. Jundub ibn ‘Abdillah (RA) has told a scene from before this. The Prophet {{2}} was first sending someone as commander, Abu ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah (RA), or ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Harith (RA). At the time of departure, out of love for the Prophet {{3}}, he wept and sat down. Then ‘Abdullah ibn Jahsh (RA) was sent in his place.{{4}}
blocks.46: The Messenger of Allah {{1}} wrote a letter for ‘Abdullah ibn Jahsh (RA) and told him not to open it before travelling two days. After two days he opened the letter and saw it was written, when you see this letter of mine, go forward and halt at Nakhlah between Makkah and Ta’if; keep watch there on Quraysh and let us know of their news. And he commanded him not to force any of his companions.{{2}}
blocks.47: A sealed letter, and with it a condition. ‘Abdullah ibn Jahsh (RA) read the letter and said, sam‘an wa ta‘atan; we heard and we obey. Then he said to his companions, he has forbidden me to force any of you. So whoever wants martyrdom, let him come with me; whoever does not, let him go back. I am going forward by the command of the Messenger of Allah {{1}}. No one went back.{{2}}

footnotes.1: Sa‘d ibn ‘Ubadah (RA) as deputy at the Battle of al-Abwa’: Ibn Hisham ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Awwal al-Maghazi’. The banner in the hand of Hamzah (RA): al-Waqidi ← Ibn Kathir (same chapter). Sirah-based.

Companions: sixty in Sirat al-Mustafa, seventy in al-Raheeq al-Makhtum. Leader of Banu Damrah: Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Hisham (vol. 2, p. 286) and Sirat al-Mustafa have ‘Makhshi ibn ‘Amr’; al-Raheeq al-Makhtum has ‘‘Amr ibn Makhshi’. Sirah-based.
footnotes.3: al-Raheeq al-Makhtum (Safiur Rahman Mubarakpuri; Bengali translation), pp. 335–336 (‘Ghazwahs and Sariyyahs before Badr’). Note 377 on p. 342: the books differ on the order and number of expeditions; the author follows Ibn al-Qayyim’s Zad al-Ma‘ad. Sirah-based.
footnotes.4: Buwat: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat Buwat min Nahiyat Radwa’; Sirah-based. Deputy in Madinah: Sa’ib ibn ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un according to Ibn Hisham, Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh (RA) according to al-Waqidi.
footnotes.5: al-Raheeq al-Makhtum (Safiur Rahman Mubarakpuri; Bengali translation), p. 339 (a hundred and fifty or two hundred Companions, thirty camels); Sirat al-Mustafa (SAW) (Bengali edition ‘all volumes together’), vol. 2, pp. 46–47 (two hundred Muhajirun, thirty camels). Sirah-based; Abu Salamah ibn ‘Abd al-Asad as deputy (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2, p. 291).
footnotes.6: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat al-‘Ushayrah’; Sirah-based, the narration of Ibn Ishaq
footnotes.7: Sahih al-Bukhari 3949 (from Abu Ishaq al-Sabi‘i; the answer of Zayd ibn Arqam (RA))
footnotes.8: ‘Ushayrah and the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam (RA): Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat al-‘Ushayrah’; in Ibn Kathir’s explanation Zayd’s ‘first’ means the first ghazwah he himself went on. Number of ghazwahs: Sirat al-Mustafa, vol. 2, p. 44: in the counting of Sirah scholars twenty-seven, from Sa‘id ibn al-Musayyib twenty-four, from Jabir twenty-one, from Zayd nineteen.
footnotes.9: The call ‘Abu Turab’ at ‘Ushayrah: Ibn Ishaq ← Yazid ibn Muhammad ibn Khuthaym ← Muhammad ibn Ka‘b al-Qurazi ← Muhammad ibn Khuthaym ← ‘Ammar ibn Yasir (RA); Ibn Kathir, ‘Ghazwat al-‘Ushayrah’. In Ibn Kathir’s words, gharib by this chain. In Sahih al-Bukhari there is another incident of calling ‘Ali (RA) ‘Abu Turab’ (sleeping in the mosque); that is a separate incident.
footnotes.10: al-Waqidi ← Ibn Jarir ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Fasl fi Sariyyat Hamzah (RA)’; narration of al-Waqidi, Sirah-based
footnotes.11: The banner: Ibn Hisham, Sirat al-Nabi, vol. 2, pp. 287–290: according to Ibn Ishaq the first banner was ‘Ubaydah’s. al-Raheeq al-Makhtum, p. 336: Hamzah’s white banner was first, the bearer Abu Marthad al-Ghanawi (RA). Sirat al-Mustafa, vol. 2, pp. 44–45. Sirah-based.
footnotes.12: al-Waqidi ← Ibn Jarir ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Fasl fi Sariyyat ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Harith’; narration of al-Waqidi, Sirah-based
footnotes.13: Leader of the Quraysh group in ‘Ubaydah’s sariyyah: ‘Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, according to Ibn Hisham Mikraz ibn Hafs; sixty or eighty horsemen; defection of al-Miqdad and ‘Utbah: Ibn Hisham, Sirat al-Nabi (Bengali translation), vol. 2, pp. 286–287; Sirat al-Mustafa, vol. 2, p. 45. al-Raheeq al-Makhtum, pp. 336–337: leader Abu Sufyan, two hundred men. Sirah-based.
footnotes.14: Sahih al-Bukhari 3728 (from Qays ibn Abi Hazim; the own words of Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas (RA))
footnotes.15: The first arrow: Sahih al-Bukhari 3728 (the own words of Sa‘d (RA)). The incident of ‘Ubaydah’s sariyyah: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Hisham, Sirat al-Nabi (Bengali translation), vol. 2, pp. 286–288; Sirat al-Mustafa, vol. 2, p. 45. Sirah-based.
footnotes.16: al-Waqidi ← Ibn Jarir ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Fasl fi Sariyyat Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas ila al-Kharrar’ (Abu Bakr ibn Isma‘il ← his father ← ‘Amir ibn Sa‘d (RA) ← Sa‘d (RA)); narration of al-Waqidi, Sirah-based

Number of Sa‘d’s group: eight Muhajirun in Ibn Ishaq’s narration, twenty or twenty-one in al-Waqidi’s. Banner-bearers: Abu Marthad al-Ghanawi for Hamzah, Mistah ibn Uthathah for ‘Ubaydah (RA) (al-Waqidi). Sirah-based.
footnotes.18: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat Badr al-Ula’; Sirah-based, the narration of Ibn Ishaq
footnotes.19: Account of the four expeditions: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah (chapters of al-Abwa’, Buwat, ‘Ushayrah, Badr al-Ula). ‘Wa lam yalqa kaydan’ (met no harm) at the end of the first three expeditions; at Badr al-Ula ‘fatahu Kurz’ (Kurz slipped from his hand). Ibn Hisham: Ibn al-Hadrami was the first person killed by the Muslims. Sirah-based.
footnotes.20: Badr al-Ula: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir. Zayd ibn Harithah (RA) as deputy in Madinah and the banner in the hand of ‘Ali (RA): Ibn Hisham and al-Waqidi ← Ibn Kathir. Ibn Ishaq–Ibn Hisham (pp. 292–293), Ibn Kathir and Sirat al-Mustafa (p. 48) place Safwan after ‘Ushayrah; al-Raheeq al-Makhtum (pp. 338–339) right after Buwat, in Rabi‘ al-Awwal. Sirah-based.

Ibn Kathir brought it as supporting evidence (shawahid) for Ibn Ishaq’s narration. ‘Fa-lamma dhahaba baka sababatan ila Rasulillah {{1}}’ (at the time of departure he wept with longing for the Messenger of Allah {{2}}).

porbos.title: That Evening at Nakhlah • I Did Not Command • The First Killing, the First Spoils • The One Who Rushed Out First • True Strength • Final Word

blocks.1: On the way a camel of Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas (RA) and ‘Utbah ibn Ghazwan (RA) went missing. The two of them fell behind to look for it. The others reached Nakhlah. There a caravan of Quraysh came. With them were ‘Amr ibn al-Hadrami, ‘Uthman ibn ‘Abdillah, his brother Nawfal, and al-Hakam ibn Kaysan. The people were frightened on seeing them. Then ‘Ukkashah ibn Mihsan (RA) came before them with his head shaved; seeing him, they were reassured. The Companions consulted among themselves. By their reckoning the day was the last day of Jumada al-Ukhra. If they let them go tonight, the caravan would enter the Haram; then they would not be reachable. They took courage. They decided that they would kill whom they could, and take what there was. By the arrow of Waqid ibn ‘Abdillah (RA) ‘Amr ibn al-Hadrami was killed. ‘Uthman and al-Hakam were taken captive; Nawfal fled.{{1}}
blocks.2: One evening. A caravan, which if it entered the Haram could not be caught. And before them a principle of the Qur’an; no fighting in the sacred month. Rajab is one of those four sacred months in which fighting is forbidden. But if someone attacks during that time, there is room to take measures of self-defence.{{1}}
blocks.3: By the Companions’ count the day was the 30th of Jumada al-Ukhra. But that very evening the moon of Rajab had risen. The sacred month was not broken knowingly.{{1}}
blocks.4: The killing happened. The moment passed. And what happened after that is the biggest part of this story.
blocks.6: ‘Abdullah ibn Jahsh (RA) returned to Madinah with the caravan and the two captives. The first words the Prophet {{1}} spoke were not words of praise.
blocks.8: The Messenger of Allah {{1}} said, I did not command you to fight in the sacred month. He held back the caravan and the two captives, and would not agree to take any of it. At this the Companions were bewildered and thought they were ruined. And their Muslim brothers also rebuked them.{{2}}
blocks.9: The returning group had the caravan in hand, but the Prophet {{1}} did not even stretch out a hand toward it. The spoils that people find dearest, he did not touch at all; because it had come from an act he had not commanded.{{2}}
blocks.10: The Companions of Nakhlah had acted with good intention, yet the Prophet {{1}} said, I did not command. Today, citing good intention, we do many things; in the name of religion, in the name of society, in the name of justice. Good intention alone does not prove there was a command. And a storm rose outside Madinah. Quraysh said, Muhammad and his companions have made the sacred month lawful; they have shed blood, taken property, taken people captive. And the Jews looked for bad omens in the meanings of the names. They said, ‘Amr means war has been made prosperous; al-Hadrami means war is present; Waqid means war has blazed up. The Companions were broken. And then a verse came down from the heavens.
blocks.12: People ask you about the sacred month, what about fighting in it? Say, fighting in it is a great sin, but turning people away from the way of Allah, adopting a disbelieving course against it, imposing a ban on al-Masjid al-Haram and driving its residents out of it is a greater sin with Allah. And fitnah is a graver thing than killing.{{1}}
blocks.13: There is balance in the language of this verse. Fighting in the sacred month is admitted to be a ‘great sin’; no concession is given. But at once it is said, there are greater sins than that; turning people from the way of Allah, preventing entry into al-Masjid al-Haram, driving out its residents. The man who was killed was killed on the basis of a misunderstanding. He was not knowingly killed in the sacred month. And those who raised a storm of criticism over this incident, their offence is far graver than this.{{1}}
blocks.14: By their own knowledge the Companions had fought in Jumada al-Ukhra itself. So they are deserving of forgiveness. To blame them is not justice.{{1}}
blocks.15: After the verse came, the Prophet {{1}} accepted the caravan and the captives.
blocks.17: Then Quraysh sent ransom for ‘Uthman and al-Hakam. The Messenger of Allah {{1}} said, we will not release your two men until our two companions return; because we fear for them; if you kill them, we will kill your two. When Sa‘d (RA) and ‘Utbah returned, the Messenger of Allah {{2}} released the captives for ransom.{{3}}
blocks.18: al-Hakam ibn Kaysan (RA) on being freed accepted Islam, and was martyred on the day of Bi’r Ma‘unah. ‘Uthman returned to Makkah and died upon disbelief. And the Companions? Those who had thought they were ruined then hoped anew.
blocks.20: They said, O Messenger of Allah, may we hope that this is an expedition for us deserving the reward of jihad? Then Allah revealed, ‘(On the other hand) those who believed and those who migrated and struggled in the way of Allah, they are certainly hopeful of Allah’s mercy. Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful’.{{1}}
blocks.21: The mistake remained a mistake. And the hope of forgiveness remained too.{{1}}
blocks.22: When we catch someone’s mistake, we either cover it or throw them away. The path between these two is hard; speaking the truth, and keeping hold of the person. At Nakhlah the Prophet {{1}} did exactly that. He said plainly, I did not command; and he also did not abandon them.
blocks.23: The First Killing, the First Spoils
blocks.24: The Muslims also answered Quraysh’s accusation in poetry. The poem is ‘Abdullah ibn Jahsh’s (RA). The first three lines are these,
blocks.26: You count killing in the sacred month a great offence; yet there is a greater offence, if only a rightly guided man could see it. Your turning away from what Muhammad says, and disbelieving in him; Allah sees it, a witness. And your driving the people of Allah’s mosque out of it, so that no one prostrating to Allah may be seen at the House.{{1}}
blocks.27: The Qur’an too said the same; admitting ‘a great sin’ and then the list of ‘a greater sin’. The poem is in that very tune. By the account of history the result of the incident of Nakhlah is many ‘firsts’.
blocks.29: Ibn al-Hadrami is the first person killed by the Muslims, and this is the first spoils the Muslims took; and ‘Uthman and al-Hakam are the first captives of the Muslims.{{1}}
blocks.30: First blood, first captive, first spoils; and the first incident after which the Prophet {{1}} said, I did not command. As if a rule was marked out at the very first step. No action without command, without limit of time; and once an action is done, accountability is direct.
blocks.31: The One Who Rushed Out First
blocks.32: In the midst of all these expedition stories, one picture of a night cannot be left unsaid. Which year exactly, is not known. But it is a picture of Madinah’s early life.
blocks.34: The Prophet {{1}} was the most handsome of people and the bravest. One night the people of Madinah were frightened; hearing a sound everyone rushed toward it. The Prophet {{2}} came and stood before them; he was returning having already got the news, on the back of a saddleless horse of Abu Talhah (RA), a sword hung round his neck. He was saying, do not be afraid, do not be afraid. Then he said, I found the horse like a sea.{{3}}
blocks.35: A sound in the night. Everyone ran toward the sound. By then he was coming back, with news. The bravest man had gone first of all and returned fastest of all. And on returning, the first thing he said was, do not be afraid. The man who had himself held back his hands for thirteen years, when the time to raise the hand comes, is in front of everyone; and before raising the hand he looks four times, is this a command? Courage is then not shouting. Courage is, one who knows when to stop, and again when to rush out first.
blocks.36: We seldom think that two things can be together within one person. The one who knows how to hold back the hands is the very one who can run first toward the sound in the darkness of night. Because both come from the same place; control over oneself. One who has no control rushes in anger, flees in fear. One who has control runs when needed, stops when needed.
blocks.38: Now the shortest, but heaviest hadith of this dars.
blocks.40: The Messenger of Allah {{1}} said, the strong one is not the one who defeats others in wrestling. The strong one is the one who can control themselves at the time of anger.{{2}}
blocks.41: Another had come and said, give me advice.
blocks.43: A man said to the Prophet {{1}}, give me advice. He said, do not be angry. The man repeated the same thing several times, and each time he said, do not be angry.{{2}}
blocks.44: An incident of another day. Two men began to quarrel right in front of the Prophet {{1}}.
blocks.46: Two men abused each other near the Prophet {{1}}, we were sitting with him. One of them was abusing his companion in anger, his face had turned red. The Prophet {{2}} said, I know a phrase that if he said it, this state of his heart would go; if he said, ‘A‘udhu billahi min al-shaytan al-rajim’. Then the people said to him, do you not hear what the Prophet {{3}} is saying? He said, am I mad?{{4}}
blocks.47: He said, am I mad? To whom anger holds, it seems this medicine is not for me. That first moment of anger comes to our homes too. A comment catches the eye on the mobile; in the name of one’s own parents, one’s own din, against one’s own opinion. The fingers start typing by themselves. A five-second reply, whose consequences go on for five years. A child made a mistake, a wife said a harsh word, a father scolded. In these small moments of the home is our first and greatest test. The Companions of thirteen years handled this very moment year after year. Can we handle just one moment? The Prophet {{1}} has taught a tiny medicine, ‘A‘udhu billahi min al-shaytan al-rajim’. That man pushed it away saying ‘am I mad’; if we do not push it away, that tiny sentence itself is the medicine. And there are some things that are plainly haram to do in a moment of anger. The Prophet {{2}} said, to abuse a Muslim is fisq.{{3}}
blocks.48: There the phrase ‘I will stop later’ does not apply; stopping right now. The haram and the habit are two separate things. Abusing, raising a lie, raising a hand against someone unjustly; these are haram. In the case of the haram there is no room to say ‘I will leave it gradually’; today, this very moment, stop. And the habit of controlling anger is built step by step; one reply fewer today, another one fewer tomorrow. The thirteen years of the Companions were a long training in this very habit. And the whole thirteen years of the Companions were the real form of this one hadith. They had the ability to raise a hand. But they did not have permission. And through that very absence of permission a kind of person was made, who even when raising the sword does not take revenge; does justice.
blocks.50: What was seen in today’s dars is a few pictures. One noon in Makkah a group of Companions, whose hands were tied; and one sentence, the command to forgive. The first expedition twelve months after coming to Madinah, whose result was a pact. A commander who did not cross the limit of a command; and that evening at Nakhlah, after which the Prophet {{1}} said, I did not command.
blocks.51: Beneath all the pictures one single word; raising the sword in hand is easy, but the habit of controlling the hand before the sword is the real lesson. Those who restrained their hands for thirteen years, when they raised their hands, they had justice in their hands. Because they knew, this is not revenge. In the next dars on the field of Badr it will be seen how that courage stood the test.
blocks.52: So take one task from today’s dars.
blocks.54: For thirteen years the Companions’ hands were tied; even when beaten they were not permitted to strike back, and that very patience made them worthy of having the sword placed in their hands. Today I will ask myself a question, in a moment of anger am I giving a just response, or only taking revenge?
blocks.55: From today for one week, in a moment of anger I will not say a single word back; this restraint I will not abandon from today on.

quiz.q: Who killed ‘Amr ibn al-Hadrami at Nakhlah by shooting an arrow?
o: ‘Ukkashah ibn Mihsan (RA)
‘Abdullah ibn Jahsh (RA)
Waqid ibn ‘Abdillah (RA)
‘Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa (RA)

quiz.q: What did the Companions take the day of Nakhlah to be by their own reckoning?
o: The first day of Rajab, thinking the moon had been seen
The last day of Jumada al-Ukhra
The last day of Ramadan, like Hamzah’s expedition
The start of Shawwal, like ‘Ubaydah’s expedition
quiz.e: Background of Surah al-Baqarah 2:217; the tafsir notes.

quiz.q: Which is correct about the Nakhlah killing, according to the dars?
o: The sacred month was broken knowingly, but the Prophet ﷺ accepted it
The people of the caravan had attacked first, hence the killing in the sacred month
The sacred month was not broken knowingly; the day was miscounted
The Prophet ﷺ had earlier permitted attack in the sacred month

quiz.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ say on seeing the returning group?
o: I have been commanded to forgive, so do not fight
Do not wish to meet the enemy
I did not command you to fight in the sacred month
Do not be afraid, do not be afraid; I found it like a sea

quiz.q: Until whose return did the Prophet ﷺ not want to release Quraysh’s captives?
o: Sa‘d (RA) and ‘Utbah
‘Ukkashah and Waqid (RA)
Hamzah (RA) and ‘Ubaydah (RA)
Abu Hudhayfah and ‘Amir

quiz.q: Which of the captives later accepted Islam?
o: ‘Uthman ibn ‘Abdillah
Nawfal ibn ‘Abdillah
‘Amr ibn al-Hadrami
al-Hakam ibn Kaysan

quiz.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ do first with the caravan and captives?
o: Held them back, took nothing
Distributed at once among his companions
Sent them back to Quraysh and asked for forgiveness
Punished ‘Abdullah (RA) in front of everyone

quiz.q: Even though the Companions of Nakhlah acted with good intention, what lesson did they leave?
o: With good intention any act becomes lawful even without a command
Without a command, intention has no value in any act
If the intention is good, no accountability for a mistake
Good intention is not enough; it is necessary to see whether there is a command

quiz.q: When there is a need to point out someone’s mistake, what is the lesson of the Nakhlah incident?
o: Covering the mistake and saying nothing
Throwing the person away completely and moving away for ever
Saying the truth plainly, and not abandoning the person
Publicising the mistake before everyone
quiz.e: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir; ‘Our Home Today’.

quiz.q: Who is the first person killed by the Muslims?
o: Abu Jahl
Umayyah ibn Khalaf
Ibn al-Hadrami
Kurz ibn Jabir

quiz.q: After Nakhlah, how did the Muslims answer Quraysh’s accusation in poetry?
o: By promising to return the caravan and the captives
By threatening to send a new expedition in the month of Rajab
By announcing the blood-money of Ibn al-Hadrami
By giving the list of the greater offences

quiz.q: In whose name is the poem composed in answer to Quraysh’s accusation over Nakhlah in the dars?
o: In the name of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA)
In the name of Hassan ibn Thabit (RA), because he was Madinah’s poet
In the name of ‘Abdullah ibn Jahsh (RA)
In the name of Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas (RA), because he was Waqid’s companion

quiz.q: According to the dars, what was the source of the Prophet’s ﷺ holding back his hands and rushing out first?
o: Knowing beforehand that the enemy were few
Desire for spoils
Fear of Quraysh
Control over himself

quiz.q: In which incident did a man say, ‘am I mad?’
o: In that other-day incident where the man who asked for advice was told again and again ‘do not be angry’
In the incident of returning on Abu Talhah’s horse at the sound of the night
In the incident of speaking about defeating others in wrestling
In the incident of teaching a‘udhu billah to the man who was abusing with a red face in anger

quiz.q: Which sentence did the Prophet ﷺ teach for the angry man?
o: Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji‘un
A‘udhu billahi min al-shaytan al-rajim
Sam‘an wa ta‘atan
Do not be afraid, do not be afraid

quiz.q: Someone said something that provokes anger; according to the dars what is the first thing to do?
o: Immediately returning the reply with equal sharpness and silencing them
Stopping; first controlling oneself, then the reply
Twisting the matter and spreading it before everyone
Setting down a reply twice as harsh as the word

quiz.q: What does the dars say about the habit of abusing?
o: Haram, so not ‘gradually’; stop right now
A mere bad habit, leaving it step by step is enough
Makruh, leaving it within a year is enough
Leaving it only in the month of fasting, and the rest of the time is permitted

quiz.q: What does the dars say about building the habit of controlling anger?
o: With firm resolve it gets built in one day without any steps
An innate nature, so it cannot be changed
It gets built as soon as permission for the sword is received
It is built step by step; one reply fewer today, another tomorrow

quiz.q: On seeing an objectionable comment about religion on Facebook, what is the dars’s lesson?
o: Stopping before replying, saying a‘udhu billah, then the just word
Raising harsh words about the commenter’s parents and past
Gathering a crowd and all pouncing together
Replying at once with abuse

quiz.q: A child has made a mistake, anger has risen; which is the dars’s most usable lesson?
o: Raising a hand at once and giving harsh discipline
Stopping in the first moment and saying a‘udhu billah
Suppressing the anger and accumulating resentment in the heart
Pointing out the mistake again and again before everyone to humiliate

quiz.q: Someone has exceeded the limit by replying in a fit of anger; which hadith is most relevant?
o: Do not wish to meet the enemy, ask Allah for safety
The strong one is the one who keeps control over themselves at the time of anger
To abuse a Muslim is fisq
Paradise is under the shade of swords

quiz.q: In the practical resolve, what is one to refrain from for a week?
o: Speaking all kinds of words
Making long du‘a after every prayer
Speaking back in a moment of anger
Meeting anyone
